title_guess: Consumer Price Index: groups, reference periods, segment CPIs, CPI rural/urban/combined, weights and calculation
running_examples: supply chain producer → wholesaler → retailer → consumer with producer, wholesale and consumer prices feeding PPI, WPI, CPI
six consumption groups with recall periods 7 days / 1 month / 1 year (MMRP)
four worker groups with baskets of about 146-365, 463, 260 and 260 items → CPI-UNME, CPI-IW, CPI-AL, CPI-RL
group weights: food 36.29 (urban), 54.18 (rural), 45.86 (combined); each column sums to 100
egg: 10 market price quotes → price relatives → elementary index 150.40 → weight 0.36 in the urban basket → Laspeyres CPI-U

best_moments.why: the screen floods with about 30 everyday purchases around one consumer, then they snap into six labelled panels: classification shown by sorting real objects
baskets shrink from a loaded trolley to a tiny bag across the four worker groups: different consumption shown by size, before any number
supply chain with a price band at each hand-over and a down-arrow from each price into PPI, WPI and CPI: where each index measures is a place on the chain
one egg followed from 10 market quotes to its elementary index, to its weight in the basket, into the CPI formula: the whole calculation traced through a single object
CPI-AL and CPI-RL arrows funnel into a handshake-over-cash icon labelled minimum wage: an index's use shown as its outcome

weak_moments.why: six short recall periods are typed one every 15-20 s beside a word list for about 115 s; no picture
quote paragraph and recommendation text box laid over a real photo of a public figure (BIE must not use real-person photos)
a weights table of 18 numbers with only boxes and a cross for emphasis; could be bars or basket shares
branded product packs (cooking oil, coffee, snacks) used as food icons
the MMRP rule lives in two text tags; no picture of a short vs long recall window

segments.teaches: goods are priced at each hand-over from producer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer; the average price level at each point gives PPI, WPI and CPI, and CPI covers goods and services

elements.what: Consumer Price Index
smoking factory (producer) → warehouse (wholesaler) → shop (retailer) → person (consumer), arrows labelled goods
coloured bands at each hand-over named producer price, wholesale price, consumer price
'services' line arching from the factory straight to the consumer
blue band 'measure average price level' along the bottom
down-arrows from each price into PPI, WPI, CPI with full names

segments.notes: channel like-counter overlay in the first 10 s (promo, ignored)
segments.idea: PPI, WPI and CPI measure prices at different points of the same supply chain; CPI is the price the final consumer pays
segments.shown_as: a smoking factory, a warehouse, a shop and a person stand in a row joined by 'goods' arrows; a coloured band drops over each hand-over and is named producer, wholesale and consumer price; a 'services' line arches from the factory straight to the person; a blue 'measure average price level' band slides in at the bottom and a down-arrow from each price drops into it as PPI, WPI and CPI

segments.teaches: CPI follows everything a consumer buys: food, drinks, rent, clothes, fuel, durables and more

elements.what: consumer person in the centre
fruit bowl, grocery bag, milk, cooking-oil can, roast chicken on the left; bottled water, coffee jar, snacks on the right

real branded food packs among the items

segments.notes: almost no words; the quantity of objects carries 'everything a household buys'
segments.idea: the consumer basket is everything a household spends on, not just food
segments.shown_as: the screen clears to a lone consumer; a bowl of fruit appears, then groceries, milk, cooking oil and a roast chicken gather at his left and drinks and snacks at his right; then the whole screen floods with everyday purchases around him: a rented house, clothes, slippers, tobacco tins, a fuel pump, gas cylinder, firewood, bulbs, a car, washing machine, fridge, necklace, chair

segments.teaches: CPI sorts consumer spending into six groups: food & beverages; pan, tobacco & intoxicants; housing; clothing & footwear; fuel & light; miscellaneous

segments.shown_as: the scattered items snap into six pale-blue panels around the consumer: groceries together, tobacco tins together, the rented house alone, clothes with slippers, fuel/gas/firewood/bulbs, and car-fridge-necklace-chair as the catch-all; a label strip is written under each panel one by one

segments.teaches: the survey asks about each group over a different recall period: food and tobacco the last 7 days, housing and fuel the last month, clothing and miscellaneous the last year

segments.idea: how often people buy something decides how far back the survey asks about it
segments.shown_as: the pictures vanish; the consumer stands over a 'consumption pattern' heading with the six group names stacked as cream chips; to the right a recall period is written beside each group, one every 15-20 s
segments.example: 7 days / 7 days / 1 month / 1 month / 1 year / 1 year

segments.teaches: the answers from the six groups, each over its own period, are pooled as consumption data

segments.teaches: a short recall period for frequent items and a long one for infrequent items is the Modified Mixed Reference Period (MMRP), consistent with international practice

elements.what: two blue tags at the top: food → shorter period; infrequent items → longer period
purple 'international practice' tag
cream panel washed over the pairs-into-database diagram
MODIFIED MIXED REFERENCE PERIOD - MMRP under the panel

segments.idea: the mixed recall method has a name (MMRP) and matches world practice

segments.teaches: consumers differ in basket size and items (choice, purchasing power), i.e. socio-economic differences; to handle this, similar consumers are grouped (segmentation)

elements.what: consumption-data cylinder → heap of dark person silhouettes topped by a red India map
line from the heap to a 'different consumption pattern' box: basket size and items vary
choice of consumption, purchasing power
socio-economic differentiation ↓ to tackle this ↓ homogeneous groups → SEGMENTATION

segments.notes: the crowd-on-map icon becomes the video's symbol for 'all Indian consumers'
segments.idea: because people buy differently, one basket cannot fit everyone, so consumers are split into similar groups
segments.shown_as: the consumption-data cylinder points to a heap of dark person silhouettes topped by a red India map; a callout from the heap opens a 'different consumption pattern' box (basket size and items vary; choice and purchasing power), then a down-arrow chain runs from 'socio-economic differentiation' to 'to tackle this' to 'homogeneous groups' and lights up the word SEGMENTATION

segments.teaches: four consumer segments: urban non-manual employees, industrial workers, agricultural labourers, rural labourers (the last two overlap)

elements.what: crowd-on-India-map at the top labelled consumer segmentation
four black silhouettes: clerk at a desk, worker with a hammer, labourer watering a field, labourer carrying sacks
short definition typed under each figure
blue box around the two rural figures with a two-way arrow between them

segments.notes: crowd at top fans out into four columns (tree without lines); figures carry the identity, definitions are text
segments.idea: CPI groups people by the kind of work they do, because work shapes spending
segments.shown_as: the India crowd moves to the top, labelled consumer segmentation; four black silhouettes pop in beneath (a clerk at a desk, a worker with a hammer, a labourer watering a field, a labourer carrying sacks), each named, then a short definition is typed under each; finally the two rural figures are boxed together in blue with a two-way arrow to show they overlap

segments.teaches: each segment has its own basket and so its own CPI (CPI-UNME, CPI-IW, CPI-AL, CPI-RL), compiled by the Labour Bureau; baskets hold different numbers of items

elements.what: a basket under each figure, shrinking left to right: loaded trolley, hand basket, paper bag, tiny bag
blue 'measure average price level' band with one CPI tag under each basket
green strip naming the compiling ministry bureau
yellow item-count tags beside each basket (146-365, 463, 260, 260)

segments.notes: basket size is a picture of consumption differences, though sizes do not match the item counts exactly
segments.idea: different baskets mean different price indices for each group
segments.shown_as: definitions disappear and a basket drops under each worker: a loaded trolley for the clerk, a hand basket for the industrial worker, a paper bag and a tiny bag for the farm and rural labourers; the blue price-level band returns with one CPI tag under each basket, a green strip credits the compiling bureau, and yellow tags show how many items each basket holds

segments.teaches: segment CPIs are used to set pay: CPI-UNME and CPI-IW fix dearness (cost-of-living) allowances for service-sector, manual and government employees; CPI-AL and CPI-RL help set minimum wages for farm and rural unskilled workers

elements.what: ? beside a small crowd-on-map icon at top-left
four worker figures in a row above the CPI band
down-arrows from CPI-UNME and CPI-IW to green cash-wallet icons labelled dearness allowance

whose pay each adjusts: foreign-firm service staff; manual workers and government employees
sectors: airlines, banking, communications
slanted arrows from CPI-AL and CPI-RL into one handshake-over-cash icon labelled minimum wage

segments.notes: uses of an index shown as money objects at the end of arrows
segments.idea: these indices decide real money: allowances for employees and minimum wages for labourers
segments.shown_as: the segmentation scene shrinks to a row with a '?' by the crowd; under CPI-UNME a down-arrow drops a green cash-wallet labelled dearness allowance with a cost-of-living strip, and the same happens under CPI-IW; callouts say whose pay each one adjusts; then CPI-AL and CPI-RL send two slanted arrows into one handshake-over-cash icon labelled minimum wage for farm and rural unskilled workers

segments.teaches: a 2001 National Statistical Commission report called segment CPIs partial indices that miss general price behaviour and recommended CPI for rural, urban and national (combined) levels; CPI-UNME was stopped in December 2010; new series base 2011-12

elements.what: real photo of the commission chair at the left edge
five suited figures at a long desk, one in red (chair), labelled National Statistical Commission
'2001' arrow to a report sheet with a tick
green 'segment specific CPIs' bar lifted by an up-arrow, with a note calling them partial indices
large quote mark and criticism paragraph
recommendation box branching into CPI-R, CPI-U, CPI-C (rural, urban, combined/national)
red cross on CPI-UNME reached by an arrow labelled Dec 2010; (2011-12) tag

segments.notes: real person photo: BIE will not use it; the committee icon is reusable
segments.idea: an expert commission found the old segment CPIs too narrow and asked for rural, urban and national CPIs
segments.shown_as: a real photo of the commission chair slides in at left beside five suited figures at a long desk (one in red) labelled National Statistical Commission; a '2001' arrow hands over a ticked report, and an up-arrow from it lifts a green 'segment specific CPIs' bar with a note calling them partial; a large quote mark brings in the criticism; the report then branches into CPI-R, CPI-U and CPI-C, and an arrow labelled Dec 2010 strikes CPI-UNME with a red cross

segments.teaches: status now: CPI-IW (base 2016), CPI-AL and CPI-RL (base 1986-87) remain as segment CPIs; CPI rural, urban and combined (base 2012) are the headline series, each with its own basket

segments.teaches: each basket weights the six groups out of 100; food weighs most in rural (54.18) and least in urban (36.29); rural has no housing weight; weights come from the MMRP survey

elements.what: six group rows × urban / rural / combined basket columns with a small weight symbol under each header
columns fill with weights one after another, each closing with a red 100
blue boxes around the three food weights
red cross in the empty rural housing cell
purple NOTE card: basket and weights prepared using MMRP

segments.notes: the basket icons from the previous segment turn into column headers
segments.idea: a basket gives each spending group a share of 100, and the shares differ between rural and urban
segments.shown_as: the baskets turn into column headers with a small weight symbol; the six group names line up as cream rows and the urban column fills with weights, then rural and combined, each closing with a red 100; the food weights get blue boxes, the empty rural housing cell gets a red cross, and a purple NOTE card slides in to say the weights come from the MMRP survey
segments.example: food 36.29 urban, 54.18 rural, 45.86 combined; columns sum to 100

segments.teaches: an item's elementary price index: for 10 market quotes take current ÷ base price × 100 (price relatives), then their geometric mean (Jevons formula); egg = 150.40

elements.what: big half-boiled egg above the table
quotation no. 1-10 with base price, current price and price relative columns
current price ÷ base price × 100, lifted by a curved arrow from the price-relative header
price-relative column shaded blue; yellow frames around the formula and the geometric-mean tag
box 'elementary price index 150.40' with 'geometric mean' tag
bottom strip naming the Jevons index formula

segments.notes: numbers are a made-up worked example on screen (prices 2-6)
segments.idea: one item's price change is averaged across many shops before it enters the CPI
segments.shown_as: a big egg sits over a numbered column of ten price quotes; base-price and current-price columns fill in, then a 'price relative' column, with a curved arrow lifting the formula current ÷ base × 100 above it; the relatives are shaded blue and arrowed into a box 'elementary price index 150.40' tagged geometric mean, and a bottom strip names the Jevons formula
segments.example: quote base 2 → current 4 = 200; egg elementary index 150.40

segments.teaches: multiply each item's elementary index by its weight, add up, divide by the total weight

elements.what: egg and its 150.40 index shrink and slide right

egg row → egg icon; index tagged I1; weight cell 0.36 boxed and tagged W
Σ(I × W) written, then ÷ ΣW added

segments.notes: symbols I and W are attached to real cells before the formula appears
segments.idea: the group index is a weighted average of item indices
segments.shown_as: the egg and its 150.40 index shrink and slide beside the urban food sub-table; an arrow joins the egg row to the egg, the index is tagged I and the egg's weight cell 0.36 is boxed and tagged W; then Σ(I × W) is written and ÷ ΣW is added

segments.teaches: doing the same with the six group weights (Laspeyres formula) gives CPI-Urban; likewise CPI-Rural and CPI-Combined
